metadata.title: Developing and validating measures for AI literacy tests: From self-reported to objective measures

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a curriculum-based AI literacy test administered to 2,380 students in six Hong Kong secondary schools (grades 7–9). The manuscript does not report the use of any complex survey design weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures, and it does not describe stratification/cluster sampling typical of international large-scale assessments. Because the analysis is psychometric validation using a Rasch model in WINSTEPS (with reliability and item-fit statistics), the paper does not provide guidance on which weight variable should be used from an ILSA-style database. For replication, analysts should treat the sample as a school-based convenience sample and rely on the reported Rasch fit, reliability (KR-20), and item-fit indices rather than population-representative weighted estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is not an ILSA-style cognitive achievement score generated via PVs; instead, the study develops and validates a binary-scored AI literacy test using a Rasch model (item difficulty and person ability logits). Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper focuses on item development and Rasch fit/reliability statistics and does not describe any imputation or deletion rule for incomplete responses. Given the absence of explicit missingness procedures, the safest interpretation is that the reported analytic sample reflects whatever response-completeness criteria were applied during test administration and scoring, without a documented statistical missing-data strategy.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were 2,380 students in grades 7–9 from six secondary schools in Hong Kong who learned AI through the AI4Future curriculum. The test comprised 25 selected multiple-choice items (binary scoring: correct/incorrect) administered online in classrooms for 30 minutes and proctored by project staff and a school teacher. The paper reports removal of 10 outliers in the school performance boxplots (post-removal model-building used data from 2,380 students), but it does not specify additional item-level or response-level exclusion rules (e.g., minimum item completion thresholds) beyond the outlier removal described.

The analytic sample includes 2,380 students from six Hong Kong secondary schools who completed a 30-minute online test consisting of 25 binary-scored multiple-choice items. Using a Rasch model in WINSTEPS, the authors report moderate internal consistency (KR-20/Cronbach’s alpha = 0.7), person separation coefficients below 2 (limited spread), and high item separation/reliability (item reliability coefficient approximately 1). Item fit statistics show infit mean squares and outfit mean squares mostly near the ideal value of 1.0 (IMNSQ ~0.89–1.16; OMNSQ ~0.78–1.27), with point-measure correlations ranging from 0.19 to 0.48 and acceptable exact/match congruence. Limitations include the absence of documented missing-data handling and the fact that the study does not use ILSA PV-based achievement outcomes or survey weights, so results support test validity/quality rather than cross-national achievement prediction. data.null_fields_interpretation: The study is an instrument-development and psychometric validation paper (Rasch model, reliability, item-fit, unidimensionality/local independence) and does not perform supervised ML prediction/classification. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms to extract, no ILSA program/cycle PV-based outcomes, and no target-variable prediction metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) reported in the Results section. The empty main_findings and confounders lists reflect that the paper’s primary contribution is measurement validity rather than predictive modeling.
